lesson.title: Confident, wrong and risky
lesson.subtitle: Match the check to what's at stake

video.title: Confident, wrong and risky
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.

chapters.label: The lab, and a letter home

scenes.visual: A list: Clear and confident; Bleach plus vinegar; A toxic gas.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A colleague printed an AI answer for a science lesson. It was clear and confident. It also said to clean the lab with bleach mixed with vinegar, and that mix gives off a toxic gas.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: when AI's mistakes become risks, and how to match your check to what's at stake.

scenes.visual: A list: It predicts likely words; Invented sources; Out-of-date rules; Weaker in some languages.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: You've seen why: a chatbot predicts likely words. Sounding sure is not the same as being checked. It can invent a source, repeat an out-of-date rule, or be weaker in a language with less text online.

scenes.visual: A list: A clumsy story: harmless; A wrong fact in a test; Wrong health advice; A wrong rule in a letter.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: At school, some mistakes are harmless. A clumsy story idea costs nothing. But a wrong fact in a test, wrong advice about a pupil's health, or a wrong rule in a letter home can hurt someone.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So use a stakes ladder. The more harm a mistake could do, the stronger the check. Low stakes: read it yourself. Medium: check it against the textbook. High stakes, like health, safety, marks, money or the law, need an expert or an official source, and a person decides.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! An AI answer tells my class which wild berries are safe to eat on our nature walk. Which check does it need?

scenes.visual: A list: Could poison a child; Asking again isn't checking; Can't check it? Don't use it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: An expert or an official guide. A wrong answer could poison a child, so this is high stakes. Asking the chatbot again only repeats the same patterns. And if nobody can check it, don't use it.

scenes.visual: A list: “The computer said so”; We'd check a stranger…; …but not a machine.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: There's a second trap, inside us. Automation bias is trusting an answer because a machine gave it. People skip checks they would never skip for a stranger's advice, just because it came from a computer.

scenes.visual: A list: Copied without reading; Something odd inside; Ask: how do you know?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: I see it with my pupils. They copy an AI answer into homework without reading it, even when it says something odd. So I ask one question: how do you know?

scenes.visual: A list: Open the sources; Numbers and names: the textbook; High stakes: ask the expert.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Some checks work well. Ask for sources, then open them, because invented sources are common. Check numbers and names against the textbook. And for anything high stakes, ask the person whose job it is: a nurse, the head teacher, the exam board.

scenes.visual: A list: An answer, cut into claims; Correct, wrong, or needs a source; Find the confident mistake.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: check the AI's answer
scenes.narration: In the app, an AI answer is cut into claims. Mark each one correct, wrong, or needs a source, and spot the confident mistake hiding among them.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. An AI drafted a letter to parents about the new exam rules. What do you do before it goes out?

scenes.visual: The summary: Sure isn't checked; Match the check to the stakes; Watch for automation bias; Can't check it? Don't use it. Takeaway: The higher the stakes, the stronger the check.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Check every rule against the official notice: a wrong rule misleads every family. Remember: sure isn't checked. Match the check to the stakes. Watch for automation bias, and if you can't check it, don't use it.

scenes.visual: A list: Draw a stakes ladder; Read out five AI answers; Low, medium or high?; How would we check it?.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: build a stakes ladder on the board. Read out five AI answers, from a poem to advice about medicine. Groups place each one on a rung, and say how they'd check it.

checkpoints.prompt: An AI answer lists the wild berries that are safe to eat on a nature walk. Which check does it need?

options.text: Read it once: it sounds sure
An expert or an official guide, and a person decides

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: a wrong answer could poison a child, so it's high stakes.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a child could be poisoned. High stakes need an expert, and a person decides.

checkpoints.prompt: An AI drafted a letter to parents about the new exam rules. What do you do before it goes out?

options.text: Check every rule against the official notice
Ask the AI if it's sure

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: a wrong rule would mislead every family, so check the official notice.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: reading well isn't being right. Check each rule against the official notice.
